name: Metribolone (R1881 / Methyltrienolone)
lead: Metribolone, also called methyltrienolone and by the code R1881, is a synthetic, orally active anabolic-androgenic steroid (AAS) and the 17α-methyl derivative of trenbolone [1][2]. It has never been approved for medical use.

It was tested clinically in the late 1960s and early 1970s as a possible treatment for advanced breast cancer in women, but development ended because of liver toxicity at very low doses [1]. Since the mid-1970s it has been a standard tool in laboratories, where radiolabelled R1881 is used as a high-affinity ligand to measure androgen receptor binding [1][3].

Outside the lab, metribolone has appeared in sports doping and bodybuilding. Reference sources describe it as among the most potent and most liver-toxic AAS; in rats it was reported at 120 to 300 times the oral anabolic potency of methyltestosterone, though Wikipedia notes that comparable potency has not been seen in humans [1][2].

paras: Metribolone is widely used as a "hot ligand" (usually tritium-labelled) in androgen receptor binding assays and as a photoaffinity label for the receptor. Its resistance to metabolism by 5α-reductase and lack of aromatisation make it convenient for this purpose [1][2]. Crystal structures of the human androgen receptor and progesterone receptor ligand-binding domains have been solved in complex with R1881 [4].

Studies in the late 1960s and early 1970s examined it for advanced breast cancer; it was reported to be effective and only weakly androgenic but caused severe liver toxicity, and it was never marketed [1].

Metribolone is a potent androgen receptor agonist. Wikipedia lists relative affinities of about 204% for the androgen receptor and 208% for the progesterone receptor, with lower affinity for glucocorticoid (26%) and mineralocorticoid (18%) receptors [1]. It has been described as a potent antimineralocorticoid (identified in 2007) and as a potent inhibitor of 3β-hydroxysteroid dehydrogenase types 1 and 2 (identified in 2010), so researchers are advised to interpret experiments carefully [1].
A 1992 in vitro study found that metribolone, which has glucocorticoid-receptor-binding properties, moderately stimulated growth of a human colon cancer cell line, unlike testosterone [5].

Binding to sex hormone-binding globulin is very low [1]. In vitro work with human liver microsomes has described several phase I products, including 17-epimers and hydroxylated metabolites, with glucuronide conjugates [2]. Empirical human pharmacokinetic data are lacking [2].

Reported effects include virilisation and hepatotoxicity [1]. Reference sources describe liver toxicity as exceptionally high, possibly reflecting its potency and metabolic stability, and the original 1966 report by Krüskemper and Noell described it [1][2]. Other effects listed for non-medical use include suppression of natural hormone production, sleep disturbance and cardiovascular strain, though these descriptions come largely from user reports and are not backed by controlled studies [2].

Metribolone is 17α-methylestra-4,9,11-trien-17β-ol-3-one, a synthetic estrane steroid. It is the 17α-methylated form of trenbolone [1][2]. It was first reported in 1965 and a 1966 paper described its preparation by alkylation of trenbolone [1][2].

The generic name is metribolone, but the scientific literature more often uses methyltrienolone or R1881 [1]. It is banned by the World Anti-Doping Agency [2]. Before the 2008 Beijing Olympics, 11 Greek weightlifters and four Greek track and field athletes tested positive for it [1]. Grokipedia states it is controlled under US anabolic steroid law [2].

No modern controlled trials of metribolone in humans have been published; its limited human investigation consists of the late-1960s and early-1970s breast cancer studies noted above [1]. Laboratory research has centred on its use as a receptor probe [3][4][5].

timeline.event: Metribolone first described in the literature [1].
Krüskemper and Noell report its liver toxicity [1].
Clinical investigation in advanced breast cancer; abandoned over liver toxicity [1].
Becomes a standard androgen receptor ligand in laboratory research [1].
Greek athletes test positive before the Beijing Olympics [1].

card.summary: A lab-standard androgen receptor ligand that was dropped as a drug for liver toxicity and shows up in doping cases.
card.note: Abandoned clinically over severe liver toxicity; WADA-banned; never approved.

quick.overview:
Metribolone is an oral anabolic steroid made from trenbolone in the 1960s. It was tried for advanced breast cancer but dropped because it damaged the liver at very low doses.

Today it is mainly a research reagent for studying the androgen receptor, though it has also turned up in doping tests and in bodybuilding circles.
quick.mechanism: It binds the androgen receptor very tightly and resists breakdown by 5α-reductase and aromatase. It also binds the progesterone receptor and, more weakly, other steroid receptors.
quick.risks: Documented effects include liver toxicity and virilisation. It has no approved use, is banned in sport, and has no controlled modern human studies.
